3.3.4.1-f12.accuracy_reason: Adulterare is used of debasing coin, and it is related to adulterium.

3.3.4.1-f2.accuracy_reason: Machaon was the Greek physician at Troy. The English stanza is Harington's version of Orlando Furioso 31.5, as the sidenote shows. The note leaves out that the couplet is Ovid, Remedia Amoris 545–6, but it says nothing wrong.

3.3.4.1-f24.accuracy_reason: Seneca, Epistulae 6.4 does read 'nullius boni sine socio iucunda possessio est'.

3.3.4.1-f28.accuracy_reason: Modern texts of Amores 3.4 read 'ni velit' and 'nec corpus servare potes, licet omnia claudas'. But 'mentem' and 'si velit' may be readings in older editions, so saying Burton himself changed the line claims more than the evidence allows.

3.3.4.1-f29.accuracy_reason: Amores 3.4.19–20 does read 'et hos unus saepe fefellit Amor', with 'hos' referring to Argus's eyes. The sidenote does point to the Ariosto lines quoted next.

3.3.4.1-f34.accuracy_reason: This is the opening line of Ausonius' epigram. In it the wife adds quicksilver, and the two poisons cancel each other out.

3.3.4.1-f42.accuracy_reason: In Valerius Maximus 6.7.1, Tertia Aemilia, wife of Scipio Africanus and mother of Cornelia, ignores her husband's affair with a slave girl. Burton's 'Tertius Aemilius' wife' is a garbled version of her name.
